utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, case number IT-95-8-T, Prosecutor versus case Dusko Sikirica, Dusko Sikirica, and Dragan Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dirk Ryneveld for the Prosecution along with my co-counsel, Ms. Julia Baly and Mr. Daryl Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Veselin Londrovic. I represent Mr. Sikirica along with my learned friend Michael Greaves. We also have Ms. Rastislava Petrovic the interpreter. I am the defence counsellor who does not speak English, and she will facilitate our communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Vladimir Petrovic, an attorney from Belgrade, along with Goran Rodic, an attorney from Podgorica. We represent Mr. Damir Dosen, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Dusan Vucicevic for Mr. Dragan Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is the beginning of this case, the first day. We start with opening statements. Before we begin, may I just inquire, Mr. Ryneveld, how long will your opening statement be?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I anticipate, Your Honour, that it will be slightly over an hour and a half, about an hour and 35 minutes is my estimate. There will be some very short video clips, and I'm conscious of the fact that I'm going to have to speak slowly so that the interpreters can follow along so I anticipate about an hour and 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be convenient then to take the break at 11.30, 11.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just inquire whether any of the Defence counsel will be exercising the right to make an opening statement at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence for Kolundzija would like to make a partial opening statement wherein we would dispute the elements of the Prosecutor's case. And, if possible, then at the beginning of the Defence case in chief, if necessary, we would, you know, describe our part of the case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the concept of a partial opening statement. The Rules provide for you the right to make an opening statement now. I believe you must decide whether you wish to make an opening statement now or at the beginning of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do wish to make an opening statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long will your statement be?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, I ask the Court's permission to have our case manager Rebecca Graham to assist us at the ELMO to place some maps, et cetera, to assist in the presentation of our opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is now my privilege to present the opening statement of the Prosecutor's case against Sikirica, Dosen and Kolundzija by outlining the evidence that the Prosecution intends to adduce. I do not intend to simply restate the contents of our pre-trial brief. I intend instead during the next hour and a half or so to outline the framework of our case and to highlight some of the material evidence that the Prosecution's witnesses will give. At the end of the trial, we submit that this evidence will leave no reasonable doubt in your mind as to the guilt of the three accused, Sikirica, Dosen, and Kolundzija. Your Honours, this is a case about ethnic cleansing, persecution, and genocide, committed in the opstina Prijedor in northwest Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in particular the creation of detention camps for the civilian non-Serb inhabitants in the area, the discovery of which in the summer of 1992 shocked the world. Serb Bosnian leaders repeatedly denied that concentration-style detention camps were in operation in any of the areas controlled by their forces. You will now see a very brief video clip of Mr. Karadzic in early August, 1992, denying that there were any detention camps for civilians in existence. 5

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those denials were shown to be false when video images of the gaunt and malnourished detainees at some of these detention camps were first broadcast on television in the summer of 1992, alerting the world that atrocities were being committed against civilians in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What will become readily apparent from the evidence that the Prosecution intends to adduce is that the individuals who were imprisoned in camps such as Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje were there as a result of a policy of wholesale persecution and ethnic cleansing of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats perpetrated at the hands of the Bosnian Serbs. This trial will focus on events that happened in the opstina Prijedor largely between April and August, 1992 when the purveyors of Serbian nationalistic fanaticism unleashed an orchestrated rampage of persecution and terror throughout the non-Serb dominated parts of opstina Prijedor. A similar campaign was waged simultaneously in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of the common purpose of the Bosnian Serb leadership in order to create an ethnically pure greater Serbia. Now, those who masterminded the enterprise to create such an ethnically pure state accomplished their objective in various ways. Some of these methods included destruction of villages, killing of the inhabitants, and forced deportation or detention of their survivors. In the context of an armed conflict which broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April, 1992, there began a widespread and systematic assault on the non-Serb civilian population. Bosnian Serb forces started military action and their soldiers and police started arresting non-Serb inhabitants. The town of Prijedor and the surrounding predominantly Muslim villages became a battleground. The non-Serb inhabitants of the town of Prijedor and the neighbouring villages were rounded up and their homes and religious centres were specifically targeted for destruction. As the witnesses will tell you during the course of this trial, their mosques were desecrated and destroyed, and their homes and businesses were looted, burned, and destroyed. To give you an idea of the kind of destruction the witnesses will relate to you in their evidence, we propose to show you a brief glimpse of the destruction. We propose to show you now a short video clip of the village of Kozarac that portrays the type of damage sustained in these villages. You will note that occasionally you will see a building that appears to have escaped the path of destruction. The evidence you will hear is that Serb homes, businesses or churches were not targeted for destruction, but only those belonging to non-Serbs. In these communities, the population was predominantly Muslim. 23

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Coming up in the video now you will see the remains of a mosque. 3

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: A primary component of the campaign by the Bosnian Serbs to create a purely Serbian state was to kill a part of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilian population and to drive the rest of the population out of the area. They targeted non-Serb political and civic leaders, intellectuals, and the wealthy. They also targeted those individuals that they claimed were extremists, such as military-aged men because they were capable of resisting the Serbs. The killing part of the campaign was accomplished either through direct military attack or through detaining members of these groups and subjecting them to conditions calculated to bring about their physical destruction. By killing many of the inhabitants outright, and detaining others in camps where many were beaten to death, starved, tortured or murdered, the Bosnian Serbs accomplished part of their objective. The remaining inhabitants were terrorized into leaving their homes and fleeing the area. They were driven out of their homes often carrying the sick, the elderly and the very young. They had little or no time or means to collect their personal possessions before fleeing the attack of their Serbian neighbours. They were too terrified to stay yet had nowhere to run. They ran in the direction of the next non-Serb village or the mountains, simply to attempt to survive another day. 1 Behind them, the advancing Serb armed forces left a trail of destruction in their wake; burning, looting and destroying the civilian inhabitants' homes and property. In this manner, the Bosnian Serb authorities displayed their genocidal intent in accomplishing their objective of creating an ethnically pure Serbian state. The ethnic cleansing of the Prijedor area did not occur by happenstance. On the contrary, it was a carefully planned and executed operation. In the early 1990s nationalistic political parties, the Muslim dominated SDA, and the Serb dominated SDS, openly pursued political power in Prijedor. Although the Muslim SDA won a majority of seats in the 1990 civic elections, Serb officials successfully resisted a reallocation of key civic positions in accordance with election results. The SDS also wanted to establish exclusive Serb control over large segments of territory in western, northern, and eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina despite the fact that many of these regions had large non-Serb populations residing within them. In the Prijedor area, the SDS began serious plans to create a separate Serbian territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina when it became clear to them that they could not keep Bosnia in the Yugoslav Federation. Tensions between Serbs and nonSerbs in the area mounted as did the steady build-up of Serb troops in the area. In March of 1992, Serb extremists seized the television tower on Kozara mountain following which the residents of the area could receive only broadcasts containing Serb propaganda and warning to Serbs that the non-Serb extremists were planning to destroy Serbs. On the 30th of April, 1992, Serb forces seized power in opstina Prijedor and encountered to meaningful resistance in the process. Non-Serb police surrendered their firearms to their Serb colleagues often at gun point. The following morning, Serb flags flew from all official government buildings and radio Prijedor broadcast that the Serbs had taken over the opstina. Over the next three weeks all civilians were ordered to surrender their firearms to the authorities. In reality, this order applied only to nonSerbs and, as you will hear from the witnesses, Serb civilians received weapons from the local authorities and the Serb-dominated JNA. Travel and communications for nonSerbs was restricted. Many nonSerbs were fired from their jobs and lost their medical coverage solely because of their ethnicity. The following document, referred to in these proceedings as Exhibit 2.12A, which is authored by the president of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Crisis Staff at Banja Luka, Radoslav Brdjanin, on the 22nd of June 1992 shows that this decision was made at the highest levels and was to be carried out by the Crisis Staffs of all the municipalities of the autonomous region of the Krajina. On the ELMO that document is now displayed, and it reads, and I am looking at the highlighted passages in the orange, "All leading positions, positions involving the access to information, protection of public property, and other positions of importance for the functioning of the economy can be occupied exclusively by personnel of Serbian nationality. This applies to all socially-owned enterprises, joint stock companies, state institutions, public enterprises, the Ministry of the Interior and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition, such positions cannot be occupied by workers who have not confirmed their Serbian nationality in the plebescite or to whom it is not yet clear that the only representative of the Serbian people is the Serbian Democratic Party. The deadline to carry out the task stated in Article 1 of this decision is 1500 hours of Friday the 26th of June 1992, and the president of the municipal Crisis Staffs will submit the reports to this Crisis Staff." Well, Your Honours, if there was any question about whether the ARK Crisis Staff was serious about implementing this policy throughout the 20 or so municipalities comprising the autonomous region of the Krajina, the question was answered in the next statement: "Failure to carry out this decision shall result in automatic suspension of the responsible persons." Thereafter, as will become obvious from the filed exhibits, the Crisis Staff gave a number of directions and orders which further marginalised the non-Serb population preventing them from taking part in public and economic organisations, by controlling internal population immigration, and by developing a plan designed to result in the so-called voluntary relocation of the non-Serb civilian population. In so doing, they drew their blueprint for the commission of genocide in part against the non-Serb civilian population of the opstina including political and civic leaders, intellectuals, the wealthy, and those who resisted the Serbs, such as military-aged males. Although the foregoing conduct was the beginning of the persecution of the non-Serb population of the opstina, for the inhabitants of the Prijedor area, the real nightmare began on approximately the 22nd of May 1992, when large-scale Serb military attacks began. During these military attacks by soldiers and police as well as paramilitary units equipped by the SDS, artillery shelling took place against non-Serb villages. The towns and villages that you will be hearing about during the course of the evidence in this trial such as Prijedor, Donja Puharska, Cejreci, Kozarac, Sivci and the villages Brdo such as Biscani, Rakovcani and Hambarine were irregularly but systematically attacked and destroyed, much like the Kozarac footage you saw moments ago. Although in some areas, the nonSerbs organised in an attempt to repel the armed attacks, by the middle of July 1992 all of these villages had eventually been overwhelmed by better equipped and armed Serb forces and in the process, countless non-Serb civilians were killed. During these attacks, men, women and children fled to neighbouring villages or the nearby forests and mountains where the majority were inevitably either shot, captured or surrendered to the Serb forces. Their homes and mosques were looted, burned or otherwise destroyed and their livestock were slaughtered. This was done so that they would have nothing to return to, to reason to come home. Upon capture, the men were separated from the women and children. Many were killed on the spot. Others were beaten mercilessly and then transported like cattle to detention camps in the region such as Keraterm, Omarska and Trnopolje where they suffered horribly and were subjected to unspeakable indignity by their Serb captors. Most of these witnesses will tell you about what happened to them personally. You will hear how they were attacked, rounded up, beaten, detained, abused, and starved. You will also hear from them what happened to those who are no longer alive to tell you their story themselves. You will hear how the three accused before you today were among the faces of their captors that made life a living hell during their time spent in Keraterm. You will hear evidence from the witnesses themselves who will tell you the details of how Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats civilians were summarily executed, beaten, sexually assaulted, and detained in a widespread, systematic and protracted matter. You will also hear how many of them were transferred to camps such as Omarska and Trnopolje where they were subjected to similar treatment or worse with the complicity of the accused, Sikirica. Your Honours, so thorough was the campaign of persecution and so massive was the consequence of this terror campaign, that you will hear that the Bosnian Serb authorities set up an interlocking system of approximately 39 detention camps euphemistically referred to by the Bosnian Serbs as collections or investigation centres. The evidence that will be presented to you in this case will focus on three of such camps: Keraterm, Omarska and Trnopolje, because detainees from Keraterm were routinely transferred from there to the other camps. The accused, Sikirica, who was charged with genocide and complicity to commit genocide as well as persecution in this case was the commander of the Keraterm camp. He maintained a list of the Keraterm detainees who were in his camp and which ones were to be transferred to Omarska. Many of those sent to Omarska camp in particular are known to have been killed and many were never heard from or seen again. In light of the interrelationship between the camps, it is submitted that Sikirica knew the likely fate of those he ordered transferred to other camps. You will hear evidence of how new arrivals at Omarska from Keraterm were singled for special treatment, including horrific beatings on their arrival at Omarska. As such, not only is he responsible for the genocidal acts committed by himself personally and by those under his command at the Keraterm camp itself, but also, with his knowledge and complicity, similar genocidal acts that occurred at the Omarska and Trnopolje camps. The acts committed at these camps, along with the prevalent conditions at these camps, played an essential role in accomplishing the execution of the Bosnian Serb expulsion campaign in opstina Prijedor. The operation of these camps in general and Keraterm in particular served a relevant function to the detention, killing, torturing, intimidating and terrorising of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croats in Prijedor. As commander of Keraterm camp, the accused Sikirica controlled an integral component of the wider persecution and expulsion campaign in opstina Prijedor in furtherance of enacting the common purpose. Camps such as Keraterm, Omarska and Trnopolje were staffed by Serb forces, including reserve police officers of the Prijedor Public Security Station along with other individuals often rotating between the camps. Some of these individuals may have been camp personnel but others such as Zoran Zigic and Duca Knezevic were granted access to the camps in order to persecute and murder the detainees. As camp commander, the accused Sikirica was responsible for the atrocities, beatings, murders and other war crimes perpetrated by these individuals. I'd like to turn next, if I may, to camp conditions. In a word, conditions at all three camps in abominable. It will become very clear from the evidence of the witnesses just how brutal conditions were. The Keraterm camp was located in a warehouse and grounds of a ceramics factory on the outskirts of the town of Prijedor itself. The following brief video clip shows the warehouse area that served as the detention site for many of the non-Serb male military-aged civilians from the Prijedor area. 17

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Coming into view now is the area of the Rooms 1, 2, 3 and 4 that you will hear about . This is the warehouse complex of the ceramics factory. Zooming into the foreground now you will see the weigh hut which served as the command centre for commander of the camp, Sikirica. And there you see a side view of the indentation. The rooms to the left of the indentation were Rooms 1 and 2, and to the right were Rooms 3, 4. These are the metal doors to Room 3. You will hear more about Room 3 and what is known as the Room 3 massacre. Shown now are some bullet holes above the door which is where certain stray bullets appear to have gone during the time of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we are going to have plans, are we, of the camp so we can follow this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. During the course of the evidence we intend to introduce documents which will assist the court. These are simply some documents that I'm using for the course of my opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. And does this have an exhibit number? It may be helpful to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We don't have an exhibit number for the video at the moment, but during the course of the trial, it is anticipated that many of the documents that I'm using in the opening, which is not evidence, will, with the court's permission, become evidence, and will be assigned a number, an exhibit number, by the court if it's admitted. Keraterm camp, Your Honours, was operated as a camp for detainees from the 23rd of May, 1992 until it closed on approximately the 5th of August, 1992. In the nearly two and a half months of its operation, it held about 1500 detainees, almost exclusively non-Serb males of military age. All of the guards were Serbs, and most if not all were officially employed as reserve police officers attached to the nearby Prijedor 2 police station. Keraterm camp was operated in a manner that resulted in the physical debilitation or death of the non-Serb detainees. Detainees were often transferred to Keraterm from other camps and were subjected to brutal interrogations. After they were processed, as their Serb captors called it, many were sent off to camps like Omarska, where they did not survive their subsequent treatment, including torture, beatings, starvation, as well as outright murder. For those who remained at Keraterm after interrogation, life was not much better. Torture, beatings, starvation, murder and massacre were part of the game plan for Keraterm detainees as well. When Keraterm was forced to close down in early August, 1992, many of the remaining Keraterm detainees were transferred to Trnopolje. When television crews attend reluctant access to Trnopolje, they captured the condition of the detainees on video. By the time an international commission composed of a team of journalists were permitted to attend the camps, the Bosnian Serb authorities had already issued instructions on the 3rd of August to the various camps to "take all necessary measures to bring the camps into acceptable, satisfactory condition within two days." I'm going to invite you now to look at the ELMO where what has been marked as Exhibit 8.4.3 will be shown. You will note that General Major Talic, who authored this military secret order, inter alia stated -- now the orange highlighted paragraph starting with the words: "Concerning this visit, take all necessary measures so to bring the camps into acceptable, satisfactory condition. That means order, cleanliness, functioning of the medical care for the prisoners, tidy evidence books concerning the reception of prisoners, their release, the register of those who died and the medical findings of the causes of death." Despite this advance warning, what the journalists captured on film, once steps had been taken to make the camps appear presentable, shocked the international community into action. Pictures speak volumes. So rather than attempt to describe the effect of the conditions on the detainees in words alone, I invite you to see the condition of the detainees for yourselves by viewing a portion of the video shot at Trnopolje in early August, 1992. Many of the detainees you see were previously detained in Keraterm. 14

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Some witnesses that you will hear, such as Jusuf Arifagic and Hajrudin Zubovic will tell you that they were transferred to Trnopolje when Keraterm was closed down and that they were in that camp when the video was made. Both will tell you that they appeared on the video and be able to identify some of the other detainees depicted in the video, some of whom did not survive to testify at this trial. When viewing this video, you will likely wonder what kind of conditions would result in people looking like this. By way of an answer, let me describe for you what I anticipate the witnesses will tell you was the typical treatment of prisoners who arrived at Keraterm. At the outset, you will hear that upon arrival, usually by bus, the detainees would be thoroughly and vigorously searched and beaten, sometimes while still on the bus or else on the camp grounds in the vicinity of the weigh hut which served as the command headquarters for the guards. This is a photograph of the weigh hut that served as the headquarters for the camp commanders and you can see the facility in the background. When I talk about the facility, it's the Rooms 1, 2, 3 and 4 area which is the left-hand side of the warehouse. Anything of value, money, jewellery, papers and other valuables would be stolen from them. During that process, they may again be beaten with rifle butts or other objects before being forced into one of the four storage rooms referred to by number, which you will be hearing about continually from the witnesses throughout the course of this trial. There they were locked behind metal doors in hopelessly overcrowded conditions. Often these rooms were so crowded that the detainees could not find space to lie down, or even to move, never mind find a bed or a mattress to sleep on. To give you an example of what I mean when I say overcrowded, the rooms, which differed in size, were used to house from about 200 up to about 450 prisoners each. In fact, in Room 2 which measured about 20 square metres, at one point the number mushroomed to 570 people when they emptied Room 3 prior to the massacre, which you will be hearing about later in the case. They emptied Room 3 and crammed those prisoners into Room 2 in order to make way for new arrivals from the Brdo area. I will return to the reason for doing that a little later on in my opening when I discuss the Room 3 massacre. The prisoners in general had to subsist on starvation rations. There was never enough food. What little food they received was provided erratically, contained little or no nourishment and was almost always exhausted before all the prisoners were fed. If they were near the end of the feeding schedule, there would be none left. Getting to the food or quickly downing it was also an ordeal. According to one witness, prisoners had to run a gauntlet of beatings with sticks and rifle butts wielded by guards and camp visitors just to get to the food. Then they were forced to eat within a minute or two when they were subjected to further beatings and had the unfinished portion of the food dumped on the ground - not that there was much to eat in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I wonder if you could help me. I'm not very familiar with square metres. Twenty square metres, in relation to this courtroom, could you give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm perhaps not the one to convert metres in terms of size, having been raised in the square yards or feet myself, but I would -- my best guess would be about half the width of this courtroom from about counsel's desk to the wall would be approximately 20 square metres. I see Mr. Vucicevic raised his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's not make an issue of it. We will get to it during the evidence no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Judge, I think I would be in a position to help you out because I grew up in one system and then went to another. 20 square metres would be about 22 square yards. So if he says -- if he says 20 square metres, that would be about one yard in length, and 22 yards -- I mean one yard in width, and 22 yards in length. That's a rather small space. I think you know the space that he's referring to is much bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. You will hear that on a good day, each prisoner would receive only one meal consisting of two very thin slices of fly-covered bread, since it had been kept near the toilets prior to being served, and a small bowl of water which occasionally had a piece of cabbage or macaroni in it. Some rooms, such as Room 1, whose inmates were better known to some of the guards, were fed more regularly than the other rooms. At the beginning you will hear that because Keraterm is literally located on the outskirts of the town of Prijedor, family members were able to attend at the camp gate to bring food. Initially certain prisoners were permitted to receive food from family members but after a week or so, that, too, was no longer permitted. Needless to say, during their detention over a period of two to three months all the prisoners lost weight, some as much as 35 kilograms. Their evidence is to the lack of food and its consequences on them is borne out in the brief video clip which you just saw. But food, or the lack of it, wasn't the only problem. Their detention was mainly during the hot summer months. They were packed like tin sardines in unbearably hot rooms without adequate water. They had no change of clothing, wearing only the clothes on their backs at the time of their capture, no washing facilities, no bedding, and with very rare exception, no medical care. In addition, hygiene was nonexistent. There were very few toilets, and the prisoners were rarely permitted to use them, running the risks of beatings when they did. When they did visit the toilet they had to wade through backed up overflowing sewage and filth. The stench of excrement and urine produced an overpowering amonia-like odour which made it difficult for the inmates nearest the toilets to even breathe. At night the prisoners were not allowed out of their rooms to go to the toilet but were forced to use barrels inside the room. As if the living conditions were not bad enough, you will hear from many of the witnesses that the prisoners were routinely subjected to interrogations which were regularly accompanied by beatings and torture. During their detention, the detainees were subjected to severe beatings and torture. During their detention, the detainees were subjected to severe beatings, torture, sexual assault and killings, in addition to other forms of physical and psychological abuse. Not only were they subjected to this inhumane treatment by camp guards but also by visitors to the camp, also by visitors to the camp such as Zoran Zigic and Dusko Knezevic, who came to the Keraterm camp for their own perverted and sick enjoyment of beating, torturing and killing the detainees. This all occurred with the knowledge and the tacit approval of the camp commanders and shift commanders charged with the responsibility of the security of the camp who were often present during the incidents. You will hear the witnesses tell you about the specific incidents they either endured themselves or witnessed being perpetrated upon their fellow detainees. The evidence will also disclose that after the Keraterm detainees were interrogated, they would be sorted into groups. Some, branded as extremists after the interrogation, would be called out by Sikirica and others, and shipped out by bus to Omarska. You will have made available to you documents entered as exhibits in these proceedings that will confirm the fact that over 6.000 such informative interviews took place at the Keraterm, Omarska and Trnopolje camps. I'd like next to address the Omarska camp. Although none of these three accused were officially attached to the Omarska camp, it is important to understand that in relation to the overall campaign of terror and persecution, and in particular with respect to the counts of genocide, and complicity in genocide with which Sikirica stands charged, Omarska camp played a significant role. I'm going to ask the Omarska photographs be put on the ELMO. Here in the photograph, on the ELMO, you can see the large industrial building, known as the hangar, in which many of the prisoners were detained. The concrete area in the foreground is the pista where the prisoners were forced to be during the day. To the right of the photo is the infamous "white house" where the extremists, many of them from Keraterm were detained, tortured and killed. Omarska was established by the Serb Crisis Staff on the 31st of May 1992 in the administrative centre of the Omarska iron ore mine located to the south-east of the Kozarac area not far from Prijedor. You can see now on the ELMO a map in blue showing the main Prijedor and there is the town with Keraterm located right on the edge of it. Then almost in the straight line, you will see Trnopolje, down to Omarska. From its inception, Omarska housed many of the local Muslim and Croat elite including political, administrative, and religious leaders, academics and intellectuals, business leaders, and others who led and influenced the non-Serb population. You will hear from the witnesses in the trial that many of the Keraterm detainees were determined, after they were interrogated, to be extremists and were transported to Omarska where they were subjected to similar overcrowding, starvation and hygiene conditions as was as Keraterm. They also suffered serious beatings, torture, sexual assaults and murders. General abuse was a daily occurrence. Battered corpses, the result of nightly beatings and murder, were visible virtually every morning before they were hauled away by truck. Many of the witnesses you will hear from in this case, either by way of viva voce evidence or by transcript, have given evidence in the concurrent proceeding against five other accused who are presently standing trial before a different Trial Chamber concerning their conduct at Omarska camp. Zoran Zigic, one of the accused standing trial in that case, was a common denominator to both camps in both cases in that he persecuted, beat and murdered inmates at both camps, travelling to each and causing terror and mayhem at each camp at next. I turn next, if I may, to Trnopolje. The Trnopolje camp consisted of a former school building, municipal centre, culture hall, and theatre located several kilometres from the town of Kozarac. It housed thousands of detainees, the majority of which were older men, women and children. There you see on the ELMO the Trnopolje complex. Although it is generally accepted that conditions at Trnopolje were not as bad as at either Omarska or Keraterm, conditions for the detainees at Trnopolje were nevertheless horrible. Insufficient food, almost no water, and filthy hygienic conditions prevailed. Dysentery was rampant. Due to overcrowding, many of the detainees had to live outside. Not only did beatings and killings occur at Trnopolje, but women and girls were frequently raped. At one stage, after Keraterm had closed on the 5th of August and many of the inmates had been transferred to Trnopolje, bus loads of men were taken to a remote location near the area known as Vlasic Mountain and systematically massacred. Trnopolje fit into the genocidal expulsion plan as a centre from which the surviving non-Serb population of Prijedor could be expelled to other parts of Bosnia or other countries. You will hear that the last 1500 internees were expelled from Trnopolje in November or December of 1992. Now, each of these camps played its own integral role in the ultimate objective of cleansing the area of nonSerbs. Some, as I said, were killed outright, some were beaten, and starved to death, and the rest were rendered destitute, homeless, and were terrorised into leaving the area, their Serb captors ensuring that there was nothing for them to return to. They were herded like cattle into trucks and buses and deported from the area and were often forced to sign documents that they are voluntarily surrendering their ownership rights to property that they left behind. It is the Prosecution's submission that as commander of Keraterm camp, Dusko Sikirica knew of the existence of the other camps and their purpose and participated in the systematic destruction of part of a group, the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilian population by sending Keraterm detainees to camps like Omarska and Trnopolje with the intention that they would be subjected to conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction. In so doing, he participated in genocidal acts and was complicit in carrying out the common purpose of the Bosnian Serb genocidal plan for the nonSerbs in the Prijedor area. So effective was this plan, and so thorough was the cleansing process that by August of 1992, when the foreign journalist visited the former Muslim town of Kozarac, not a single Muslim family remained. The American television news programme Nightline sent a camera crew to Kozarac after the destruction and ethnic cleansing of that village and this is a brief excerpt of the report they filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If there remains any question as to the intent of the Serbs to cleanse the area of nonSerbs, it is significant to note that they even renamed Kozarac from its former Muslim name to a new Serbian name, Radmilovici, after the Serb who led the attack on Kozarac. Other examples of how the Serbs tried to cleanse north-west Bosnia of any Muslim influence can be seen in their renaming of Bosanska Krupa, as Krupa-na-Uni, Bosanska Gradiska as simply Gradiska, and Skender Vakuf as Knezevo. Before April 1992, the population of Prijedor was almost evenly divided between Muslims and Serbs, with a slight majority of Muslims. According to the 1991 census, before the war, the opstina Prijedor had a total population of 112.470 people of whom 44.000 were Muslims, 42.5 per cent Serbs, 5.6 per cent Croats, 5.7 per cent classified as Yugoslavs and the remaining 2.2 were a mixture of Ukranians, Russians and Italians. You will see on the ELMO, a map of Prijedor which is in the middle, and you will also see the multicoloured dots, the green being the Muslim and the purple being the Serb villages. You will see the concentration around Prijedor which is the centre circle and the other little villages. While the opstina -- within the opstina, certain towns or villages would be predominantly Muslim or Serb in its ethnic composition. You will hear or read about demographic evidence to be enter at this trial concerning the ethnic composition of Prijedor's pre-war and post-war populations. By way of a preview, I invite you to look at the graph on the ELMO which compares population figures in Prijedor prior to the armed conflict from the 1991 census with the post war census taken in 1997. From the following graph, you will note that in 1991, Muslims and Serbs were equally represented in the population of Prijedor with each group at about 43 per cent. That would be the crossed hatch marks in red and green. By 1997, however, Serbs were in the majority at 89 per cent, that's the solid red one, where the Muslims are at only 1 per cent, hardly shown on the map, and the Croats at 2 per cent. It cannot escape notice that Muslims in the opstina Prijedor dropped by 42 per cent to only a negligible figure. The Bosnian Serb authorities themselves carried out a population census in 1993, just a year after the attack, presumably to see how successfully their plan had been carried out. On the 5th of August 1993, the chief of the Banja Luka security services centre wrote to officials in Prijedor asking 10 specific questions. Questions 4, 5 and 6 are particularly relevant here because they deal with the number of Serbs, Croats and Muslims then left in the opstina Prijedor. If we can display Exhibit 9.16 on the ELMO, you will see there that there are -- that's the document I referred to dated the 5th of August 1993 and the questions at 4, 5 and 6 are the total number of Serbs, the total number of Croats and the total number of Muslims. If we can go to 9.17, the answer was forthcoming two days later from the chief of the SJB in Prijedor. The answers correlate directly to the 10 questions posed in the previous document; note the figures opposite numbers 4, 5 and 6. You will note that the figures provided by the Prijedor SJB to the Banja Luka CSB on the 7th of August 1993 report, inter alia, that the total number of inhabitants of the municipality is 65.551 of which 53.655 were Serbs, 3.169 were Croats and 6.124 were Muslims. It shows in the less than two years since the 1991 census, the percentage of the nonSerbs in Prijedor had dropped from just over 48 per cent to approximately 14 per cent while the percentage of Serbs had risen from 44 per cent to nearly 82 per cent. If there is any remote question about what the object of the exercise was, a document entered in these proceedings as Exhibit 3.48 removes all potential lingering doubt. May we have 3.48, please. You will see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You explained earlier that what you say at the moment is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you explained that you didn't have Exhibit numbers for your videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it that numbers have been attributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: To those videos, no, they have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. The other matters are exhibits to which numbers have been attributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are not of course exhibits yet because they have not been entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I have referred to them as exhibits. However, that may be -- they have been filed and numbers have been attributed, and they have been provided to the court and learned counsel with numbers in order to make some sense of them. They do not become exhibits until the court declares them to be exhibits during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it's convenient at this stage to refer to them at exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because otherwise, it's totally disorderly but we just ought to understand the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and thank you for the clarification. It was for ease of reference rather than by presumptuousness that these documents were exhibits, that I am referring to them as exhibits. Returning, if I may, to the document which has been given a number as 3.48, you can see that in October, 1992, Dusko Jelisic, a Serb official from the National Security Service from the Banja Luka CSB, in an official secret document, reported that in Prijedor, "Both the official authorities and the citizens themselves are relaxing under the impression that with the departure of Muslims and Croats, everything has been accomplished." He had earlier reported in the same document - and I'm going to highlight those areas in orange, "The security situation in the Prijedor municipality started deteriorating in May, 1992, the month that saw the beginning of fighting in Prijedor area." Referring to selected highlighted passages of that report, you will note, "Dozens of villages have been almost completely destroyed and left uninhabited." He then lists the names of many of the towns and villages relevant to this trial. It is interesting to note that every village mentioned in the report is a Muslim village. "This destruction saw the beginning of the mass exodus of both Muslims and Croats. According to estimates roughly 38.000 Muslim and Croat citizens have left the municipality of Prijedor so far." And then skipping again, "As these people left, there began a massive looting of their property which was left entirely unguarded by either the owners or the municipal authorities." Skipping further down the page, "This entire period is characterised by the blowing up and destruction of buildings owned by Muslims and Croats as well as of places of worship." Then near the bottom of that page, "The military police in the town are doing almost nothing about this problem which may have negative effects later." And then on the last page at the top comes the clincher. Remember that this document is authored by a Serb national security official in Banja Luka in October of 1992. "As time goes by, one can feel that both the official authorities and the citizens themselves are relaxing under the impression that with the departure of the Muslims and Croats, everything has been accomplished." The intention, in our submission, cannot be expressed much more clearly than that. You will be hearing specific detail from the various background witnesses as to how this ethnic cleansing campaign was carried out. You will also have available to you statistics and demographic reports indicating how former Muslim areas were totally cleansed and the types of people that were most likely to go missing. You will find that in the opstina Prijedor, both the Muslim and Croat military-aged men and the best-educated individuals, the potential leaders, went missing in very high ratios. This evidence will drive you to the irresistible conclusion that there was a particular targeting for the extermination or destruction of a particular group within the Muslim and Croat population of Prijedor, which amounts to a clear genocidal plan. I'd like to turn next, if I may, to the accused. First of all, Dusko Sikirica. Dusko Sikirica was born on 23rd of March, 1964 in opstina Prijedor. During the relevant period of the indictment, then 28 year old Sikirica was the commander of Keraterm camp and was therefore in a position of superior authority to everyone in the camp, including the shift commanders, two of which included his co-accused Damir Dosen and Dragan Kolundzija. As commander of the camp Sikirica had the authority to alter the conditions of confinement that existed in Keraterm. He had the authority to select the shift commanders under his command, and had both the opportunity and the duty to prevent violations of international law from occurring in the camp, and to discipline personnel or visitors who committed those violations. Sikirica personally participated in the campaign of persecution against the non-Serbs in the Prijedor opstina. Witnesses will tell you that he was present at road checks when the non-Serb population were being driven from their homes. Additionally, when Keraterm commenced operation, Sikirica became camp commander, and during the period of its operation until it was closed down in early August, 1992, Sikirica personally committed beatings and killings of a number of prisoners. As camp commander, he had firsthand knowledge of the intolerable camp conditions, the beatings, rapes and murders of detainees that took place at Keraterm. He not only failed to prevent those crimes from happening but participated in many of those acts, and failed to report or punish those individuals who committed them. Furthermore, by operating Keraterm camp, he, in conjunction with other Serb authorities, including the commanders of the other camps, contributed to the efficient execution of the Serb strategy or common purpose to create an ethnically pure region. In the context of what occurred in opstina Prijedor, that conduct amounted to not only persecution but to genocide or complicity in genocide. Dusko Sikirica's involvement in the campaign was concurrent with his activities as commander of Keraterm. Certain witnesses will tell you that Sikirica was involved in the ethnic cleansing of the village of Hambarine and the killing of its Muslim and Croat inhabitants. On the 12th of June, Serb forces attacked the village of Hambarine. Sikirica was identified as one of the individuals who took part in the attack and looting of Muslim houses. The men and the women were separated and their valuables, jewellery and money were confiscated. According to one witness Sikirica was present when these men were taken away. In Mujadzici, a part of Hambarine, some 30 men were collected and 28 of them were killed. One of the two survivors was a former workmate of Sikirica at the Celpak factory where they had both worked before the armed conflict broke out. When Sikirica recognised him in a group of five or six men who had been selected to be taken away and killed, he singled him out and told him to run away to wherever he could. The others were not so fortunate. They were never heard from or seen again. Although that incident may show that Sikirica made a decision to save a former workmate from certain death, and is therefore exculpatory in nature, nevertheless the same evidence shows that Sikirica was involved in the process of ethnic cleansing. He chose to save one person that he knew, knowing that the others were selected to be murdered. It shows his knowledge of an impending death plan. It also shows that he was not only the commander of Keraterm but that he was an active participant in the rounding up of civilians in the Hambarine area and the execution of the ethnic cleansing campaign. I'd like to turn now to Sikirica as a camp commander. It is submitted that you will have no difficulty in concluding that Sikirica was the camp commander of Keraterm, starting sometime in early June 1992. Most of the witnesses will tell you that it was a matter of common knowledge. The witnesses will tell you that they could deduce this fact from their observations, from what the guards told them, and also the fact that Sikirica himself told some of the detainees that he was the commander in charge of the camp. You may conclude that he was not the commander when the camp first opened in May, 1992, but that he assumed command after a week or so of its initial operation, and during the time relevant to this indictment. You will hear from the witnesses that conditions at the camp became worse after Sikirica took over. You will hear the witnesses tell you that Sikirica was usually present during the day shift, especially when the detainees first arrived at the camp. He was present for their welcome to the camp, consisting of beatings and robbery of their valuables, and despite the fact that these incidents occurred on a regular basis, he did nothing to stop them and at times encouraged their commission or personally participated in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sikirica also was the man who controlled the selection of transfer of prisoners from the camp. He prepared and kept a daily list of names at his office in the weigh hut shown in the photographs from where he controlled the activities at Keraterm. And there you see the warehouse again with the hut with the flat roof, the white roof. The witnesses will tell you that he would read out lists of names and decide the fates of who would be beaten, who would be transferred to Omarska, or who would be loaded on to trucks for destinations then unknown to the other prisoners. Sometimes under the guise that they would be taken to work somewhere, prisoners volunteered to get on the trucks. They never returned. Many of their bodies have since been found in graves, about which you will hear later on in the evidence. The autopsy and exhumation reports are available to you and will explain their disappearance. Not only did Sikirica bear responsibility for the atrocities carried on in Keraterm by virtue of his command responsibility, but also by his -- by virtue of his personal participation in them. His conduct covered the gamut of war crimes. You will hear evidence of his involvement in beatings, persecution, murder and rapes. At least two of the witnesses the Prosecution is calling, Witness K and Witness U, will tell you that they were raped during their brief stay at Keraterm. One of the women will tell you that Sikirica himself was one of the individuals who punched her in the eye and raped her. Various witnesses will relate different incidents of having seen Sikirica personally murdering detainees. Among the incidents you will hear the witnesses tell you about, we expect, will include the following: First of all, Salko Saldumovic will tell you about an incident he witnessed where Sikirica shot a prisoner with his pistol. Another witness will corroborate that incident. Witness K6 will tell of an incident where Sikirica took out his pistol and shot a man up to three times in the back. A few hours later, Witness K6 saw the body of the unfortunate man where it had been dumped near the garbage bins. Witness K43 will tell you that he saw Sikirica beat a detainee who needed medication, and on another occasion he saw Sikirica shoot an injured detainee who was complaining of pain and asking for medical attention. According to the witness, Sikirica took a guard's automatic rifle and fired a few bursts into the suffering man. Again, according to the witness, he then asked the corpse whether that helped the pain. The same witness will tell you that on another occasion he noted that a prisoner was questioned by Sikirica as to why he had a small bag with him. When the prisoner told him he was a diabetic and needed his needles and insulin, Sikirica claimed the man was a "Ustasha medic" and threw the bag away. The detainee died a few days later in great pain, asking for insulin with his dying breath. Various witnesses, including witnesses K35, K3, K30 and K32, will tell you that Sikirica was the one who read out a list of some 120 or more detainees who were loaded on to buses destined for Omarska. The detainees were beaten in Sikirica's presence while boarding the buses. These detainees were never seen again until their bodies were found in a mass grave. Finally, you will hear of Sikirica's role in the Room 3 massacre. Sikirica was present when the prisoners were moved out of Room 3 into the other rooms prior to the incident. The day following the massacre, a large truck or lorry arrived and parked directly in front of Room 3. Sikirica supervised the disposition of the bodies, directing that the dead be piled aboard the truck and about 30 severely wounded be unceremoniously loaded on top of the pile. After the truck left for Omarska, a high pressure hose was brought in to wash down the area. Sikirica was heard to say that no blood was to remain behind. You will also hear that on the morning after the Room 3 massacre, Sikirica was present and personally participated in the execution of some of the remaining survivors of that massacre. Turning next, if I may, to Damir Dosen also known and most often referred to as Kajin. Like Sikirica, Damir Dosen, Kajin, was a Serb born in opstina Prijedor. He was born on the 7th of April, 1967, so that during the period relevant to the indictment, he would have been 25 years old. He was a shift commander under the command of Sikirica. When Sikirica was away from the camp during Dosen's shift, Damir Dosen was in charge of the security of the camp and the welfare of its inmates. Yet during his shift, the witnesses will tell you that many beatings, tortures and even murders took place. Damir Dosen, according to a number of witnesses, took part in many beatings and assaults on inmates at Keraterm. He was present when guards on his shift beat, tortured and murdered prisoners. He not only failed to prevent or report such criminal acts, but often encouraged such acts by participating in them. The witnesses are expected to tell you that Damir Dosen was more commonly referred to, as I said, as Kajin. He was one of the shift commanders along with Kolundzija and Fustar, and all of them, as I said, were under the command of Sikirica. Many of the witnesses will undoubtedly indicate that they did not see Kajin or Dosen personally beat anyone. Some will tell you about incidents where they thought he intervened on behalf of the prisoners or indicated "that's enough" when he witnessed the guards beating the prisoners. Nevertheless, it is very clear from the evidence we expect you will hear that Dosen was involved in the beating of prisoners personally and was present when individuals, including guards that he supervised on his shift, beat prisoners. He had the power to improve conditions but, despite being fully aware of the suffering of the detainees, chose in most cases not to do so. Many will tell you that he often appeared under the influence of alcohol while on duty. We anticipate that a number of the witnesses will relate specific incidents that they personally experienced or saw when Kajin was involved in beatings of prisoners and even killings. Some will attribute beatings committed by the Banovic brothers, themselves indicted along with these three accused but as yet not in custody, to have been committed while they were guards, according to some witnesses, under Dosen's command on his shift. More particularly, I expect you will hear that Kajin was involved in a number of incidents among which are: One, the beating on his arrival at Keraterm of Jovan Radocaj, the sole Serbian detainee held in the camp and the subsequent killing of Radocaj that same night; two, the beating of Adem Jakupovaic and Nihad Krivdic; three, the cutting with a knife of the hand of Ahmet Gutic; four, the beating of (redacted); five, the beating to death of (redacted); six, the beating of (redacted); seven, the beating to death of Drago Tokmadzic. As you might anticipate, not all the witnesses saw or heard the same events. Not all of them were in a position to see the incidents noticed or experienced by others. In fact, some witnesses will tell you that their impression was that Kajin was not the worst shift commander. Others will say Kajin's and Fustar's shift were worse than Kole's shift. It is likely that you will find that he did show some mercy and compassion for some of the prisoners from time to time. The witnesses will tell you of some of the specific examples that they noted. Some will tell you that when they were present, Kajin did nothing to stop the beatings. Others will tell you that on occasion, he did prevent further beatings. On some occasions, he stopped unwelcome visitors such as Duca, Knezevic's nickname, from entering the camp where he and Zoran Zigic used to come at will for their sadistic entertainment. Nevertheless, it's the Prosecution's respectful submission that when Dosen's conducts is viewed as a whole, it will become apparent that he, like Kolundzija, was a shift commander who had a responsibility for the welfare and safety of the prisoners at Keraterm while his shift was on duty. Not only did he personally participate in beatings, but he allowed his men to physically assault, beat, and even murder the inmates. Not only was his conduct that of a participant in those criminal acts, rendering him guilty under Article 7(1) but also as a commander under Article 7(3) of the statute. As a commander, he set a very bad example. He failed to report or punish those under his command, he encouraged them in their commission of criminal offences. As such, at the end of the case, it is our submission that you will have no difficulty whatsoever in finding him guilty of persecution under Article 5 of the statute as well as of outrages upon personal dignity, a violation of the laws or customs of war, under Article 3. Next, Dragan Kolundzija known as Kole. Dragan Kolundzija referred to by most witnesses in this case by his nickname Kole, was born on the 19th of December, 1959. At the time relevant to this indictment, he would have been 32 years old. Prior to becoming one of the three shift commanders at Keraterm in his civilian life, Kole had been a truck driver. When Keraterm commenced operation, Kolundzija started his duties as a guard but soon was promoted to shift commander, a position he held until the camp closed its doors in early August. It was during his shift on the fateful night of the 24th of July, 1992, that the infamous Room 3 massacre occurred. You will hear witnesses tell that prior to the massacre, Serb forces set up at least two machine-gun nests on the ground of the Keraterm camp facing in the general direction of the metal doors of Room 3 where in excess of 200 prisoners from the Brdo area were being detained. During the night, while the accused Dragan Kolundzija was the shift commander, the Serbs began shooting the machine-guns into Room 3 through the metal doors. The prisoners were tightly packed into the room and when the machine-guns opened up, literally like shooting fish in a barrel, the results were particularly gruesome. The carnage continued off and on for hours. The bodies of many of the victims were literally shot to pieces. Stray bullets also penetrated Rooms 2 and 4 on either side of Room 3, causing occasional casualties in those rooms as well. When the consequences of the massacre were seen the next morning, witnesses saw huge piles of bodies and body parts stacked outside of Room 3. Camp officials including Damir Dosen, asked for volunteers from among the detainees from the other rooms to load the bodies into trucks. Although the precise number of victims of the Room 3 massacre is unknown, witnesses who counted the bodies being loaded estimate between 147 to 180 being murdered, with another 50 or so seriously wounded. Many of the wounded were subsequently unceremoniously dumped on top of the pile of dead bodies and were hauled away. None of these people were ever seen again alive. But that is still not the end of that obscene event. Later the following day, the 25th of July, the accused Sikirica, claiming that the massacre was a response to an attempt by the Room 3 detainees for trying to escape, ordered the selection of some 25 survivors to be lined up outside the room. They were told to lie on their stomachs on the grass, whereupon Sikirica personally shot and killed at least one of the prisoners, and was present and participated in the cold-blooded execution of the rest of them. The second massacre occurred on the 25th of July, the day after the original Room 3 massacre. Kolundzija's role in the Room 3 massacre. Now, one of the key issues for you to determine in this case, in our submission, at least in relation to the accused Kolundzija, is the extent of his role in this massacre. The fact that this massacre occurred will not present you with any difficulty at all, we respectfully submit. The evidence will prove to be overwhelming. The fact that it happened during Kolundzija's shift will also not prove to be difficult. In fact, I anticipate that the accused will not take issue with that allegation. What will be a matter for you to determine, based on the evidence, is the exact role that Kolundzija played during the course of the massacre itself. The reason I'm highlighting this issue in my opening address is because in the Prosecution's case, you will hear many witnesses giving conflicting or contradictory evidence about the nature of the role that Kolundzija played that night. It is, of course, for you to determine the facts based on that evidence. Some witnesses will tell you that Kolundzija was heard to be yelling at the soldiers to stop shooting. Others heard him say words to the effect not to shoot at Rooms 1 and 2 because those people were innocent. Still others heard him say not to fire at Rooms 1 and 2 because those housed people from Prijedor who had already been interrogated. According to other witnesses, Kolundzija was present when the machine-gun nests were set up outside room 3. Still others attribute to him the order to form a semi-circle at a certain place in front of Room 3. Yet another witness heard Kole say, "Do not shoot at the other rooms, it is well known where to shoot." Now, if you accept that evidence, Dragan Kolundzija or Kole bears responsibility as the shift commander present for one of the worst massacres to have occurred during the entire Bosnian conflict. What exactly was said that night by Kolundzija may be difficult to ascertain. That is a matter for this Court to decide, if necessary. What will become fairly clear, however, is the gist of what Kolundzija said. He was telling the people shooting not to shoot at Rooms 1 and 2. You may even conclude from the evidence that he stood in front of those rooms and attempted to order and plead with the people firing the machine-guns to stop shooting. You may, however, also conclude from this same evidence that he was concerned about innocent people in Rooms 1 and 2 being shot at but that they were supposed to shoot at Room 3 instead. Yet another witness will indicate that he was told by the accused Dosen after the massacre that all prisoners in Keraterm were supposed to have been killed that evening but thanks to Kole and God, it did not happen. However, these pieces of evidence must be factored in with other anticipated evidence. It must be remembered that the prisoners in room 3 had been singled out for particularised treatment since their arrival because they were from the Brdo area. The men from this area were labelled as extremists because they came from an area where armed resistance to the Serbs took place. Therefore, special preparations were made for their arrival at the Keraterm camp. Just prior to their arrival, the existing detainees then housed in Room 3, were all removed and jammed into the other rooms. When the prisoners from the Brdo area which included such villages as Carakovo, Biscani and Hambarine arrived on or about the 20th of July 1992, they were subjected to particularly cruel treatment. On arrival they were forced to kneel in the hot, relentless sun and given no water. They were not given food or water for a number of days, were not allowed to get fresh air, and were locked down in the stifling hot room for days. With the rotation of the three shifts at Keraterm, Kolundzija would have had to have been on duty for a number of those shifts when the prisoners were badly treated. Factored in with the evidence concerning the night of the 24th of July 1992, the night of the Room 3 massacre. You will also hear other evidence concerning the accused Kolundzija or Kole as it relates to conditions during his shift. Although I anticipate that you will hear evidence that things were better during his shift, that there were fewer beatings, that he often prevented visitors from beating the prisoners, make no mistake about it, even during his shift, life for the prisoners was horrible, conditions were terrible. There may have been fewer beatings, but some beatings still occurred. The room 3 massacre aside, there may have been fewer deaths but they were still deaths. The prisoners may have preferred his shift, but when one compares or contrasts two evils, both are still evil only one is less so. Regardless of your findings concerning the exculpatory evidence concerning Kole or Kolundzija that will permeate the Prosecution's case or his role in the room 3 massacre, at the end of the case, you will, in our submission, conclude that in any event, he is at least guilty of persecution. If you find that he did improve the conditions for some of the prisoners, he did not do it for all of them. He played favorites. He allowed better treatment for some, but allowed horrible things to happen to others. The fact that he was able to alleviate conditions for some only goes to prove that he had the power to alter conditions for all but that he chose not to. Knowing how bad things were at Keraterm, he accepted promotion from guard to shift commander. On the one hand, it gave him the opportunity to grant privileges to certain prisoners. You will hear the times when he did so. But on the other hand, he was not uniformly magnanimous. All the prisoners suffered, but some got special privileges thanks to Kole. But he could have and should have done more for the remaining prisoners. The fact that he did not do so, also clothes him with liability for persecution. But Your Honours, not all of the witnesses will speak well of Kole. Since beatings of prisoners was a routine event at Keraterm, the shift commanders including Kolundzija were present during those beatings. Some prisoners saw or heard Kole call prisoners out of their rooms. When these men later returned, they did so beaten or bloody. Sometimes after people were beaten, Kolundzija would ask the guards why they had done that. But no one was ever disciplined or removed from the camp as a result. Although most witnesses say that fewer beatings took place on Kolundzija's shift, the overall conditions in the camp on his shift were as terrible as during the other shifts. Several witnesses recall at least four occasions when Kole was present during beatings. More specifically, witnesses will tell you that Kolundzija was present and participated when prisoners were beaten with iron bar, rifles, bats, planks and batons. One recalls an incident where Kole ordered a prisoner to go outside. Shortly afterwards, two shots were heard. Even more particularly, one witness will tell you that Kolundzija beat him with a stick. He claims that, along with two other prisoners, he was beaten by Kolundzija until he lost consciousness. We expect you will hear from witnesses that Kolundzija was also present when the Banovic brothers and a guard named Grujin would beat the prisoners while they were eating. From this and other evidence, at the end of the case you will have to decide which facts you will accept. On the whole of the evidence, however, we submit that you will be left with no reasonable doubt. You will be satisfied that Dragan Kolundzija is guilty both under Article 7.1 and under 7.3 for the conduct of individuals under his command, for the various crimes of persecution under Article 5, as well as outrages upon a personal dignity, a violation of the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute with which he stands charged. I am prepared to proceed or we can take a brief break.
