utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I indicated before the break, I'd like to turn next, if I may, to the closing of the camp. As I mentioned at the outset, it was not until the media manoeuvred their way into the Prijedor area and took video footage of the camps that the Bosnian Serb authorities were forced to close them down. Well-known newspaper journalists such as Edward Villiamy who later authored the book "Seasons in Hell", based on his observation while covering the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and Penny Marshall with her television crew who attended some of the detention camps in the Prijedor area were indirectly responsible for the closing of Keraterm and eventually Omarska and Trnopolje. You've already seen a very brief clip of the now-famous footage of Trnopolje camp earlier during the opening statement. This footage came about when western journalists, who had been demanding to have access to Prijedor to report on what they had heard to be civilian detention camps, finally received permission to do so from Mr. Karadzic. In preparation for their visit, the authorities decided to close down Keraterm. The majority of the detainees in Keraterm were transferred to Trnopolje where the conditions, although still very bad, were comparably somewhat more presentable. There they were reunited with detainees from Omarska who were also transferred there when that camp was closed. Many of the prisoners visible in that short Trnopolje clip that you saw had recently been transferred there from their earlier confinement in Keraterm or Omarska. It appears as if both the Keraterm camp and the Omarska camp were closed on or between the 5th and the 8th or thereabouts of August 1992. Not all of the Keraterm prisoners were fortunate enough to simply be transferred to another camp. You will hear from witnesses such as K31, AE, K6, K30, and K13, that two bus loads of detainees, many of whom were young military-aged men, were transported to an isolated spot and summarily executed. Sikirica called out these prisoners by name from a list, and he supervised their transport from the camp. One witness, K42, recalls the names of a substantial number of the young men who were called out to be taken away. The fate of the young men unfortunate enough to be selected by Sikirica to board these buses remained unknown until December of 1998 where their remains were found piled in a heap in a cave at Hrastova Glavica near the village of Podvidaca. If you look at the ELMO, there is a photograph of the pile of bones at the bottom of the cave. You will read in the expert witness reports that the majority of the remains found at Hrastova Glavica exhibit gunshot wounds suggesting that they had been executed by means of firearms. What's on the ELMO now is a photograph with a bullet in the skull, and near the top of the photograph, you will see what appears to be an entry wound of a bullet hole. In addition, one witness, K12, is expected to tell you that he met up with one of the passengers of those fateful buses. From him, he learned how the prisoners who had been called out were loaded on to the two buses and, after taking a circuitous route, they took in a number of camps, including Omarska, and ended up in a forested area near a cave. There they were met by armed guards who were waiting for their arrival. They were shot four by four and dumped into that cave. Witness K12 was told by the survivor Ibrahim Ferhatovic that he was hit in the hand and fell into the cave where he escaped detection. Ferhatovic told Witness K12 of the names of some of the persons who were on the bus with him who were killed. Both Ibrahim Ferhatovic and many of the people he recalls, were among the people listed by Witness K42 as having boarded the buses. Unfortunately, Ibrahim Ferhatovic was later recaptured by the Serbs and did not survive the second arrest to be able to testify at this trial. His account of what happened will have to be recounted for you by Witness K12. You will also hear from witnesses and read in the expert reports of Pasinac, which became the final resting place for many of the unfortunate civilian detainees from Keraterm and other camps. One witness, K41, will tell you that after the war her husband who was murdered in Keraterm was exhumed from a grave in Pasinac and his remains were positively identified. Another witness, K36, will provide additional details as to how the husband of K41 and many other victims of Keraterm camp ended up in unmarked graves in Pasinac either individually, or as in the case of the unfortunate victims depicted in the following photograph, crammed together in death as they had been in life in Keraterm. The photograph doesn't show it very well but - at least not on the ELMO, but there is actually visible remains of three bodies in one single grave, just on top of each other. That was grave PC13. Another example of individuals surviving execution style massacres will be recounted to you by Emsud Garibovic. Like Ferhatovic, although at a different site on a different date, he survived such a massacre. From his transcript evidence given in the Omarska case, you will be able to determine that on 21 August, 1992, he was part of a large convoy of detainees from Trnopolje who were loaded on to buses supposedly destined for Travnik. Many of the young men on those buses were separated from the rest and taken to a remote site on Vlasic Mountain, lined up along the cliff and then machine-gunned and dumped over the edge of the cliff. This execution was committed by reserve police officers from Prijedor. Incidentally the same organisation to which the three accused in this trial belong. Garibovic, along with a few fortunate others, survived in order to be able to tell you what happened to them and their less fortunate fellow detainees. You see, the thing about slaughtering people in batches with machine-gun fire and automatic weapons, although very quick, impersonal and generally effective, there is a problem for the perpetrators in that not everyone is killed outright. Many are severely wounded and die later but yet others survive among the pile of corpses and live to tell you about their experiences. These three representative samples of what occurred in these three camps show that there was an interrelationship between the camps. Prisoners were transported from Keraterm to the others where the conditions were similar. Buses or transportation had to be arranged. Some administrative organisation took place. These things did not happen in splendid isolation. People were interrogated, sorted. Lists were prepared of names. Lists were called out. People were selected for particular treatment. Some were transported to other camps. Some were murdered. Some were beaten. Some were spared. Some received preferential treatment. Some were loaded on buses and taken to be executed en masse. This happened not only at Keraterm but at Omarska and Trnopolje as well. All of this shows, in our submission, that there was a larger common design of which Keraterm was but a part. Each camp played its particular role in fulfilling the overall genocidal conduct that was perpetrated on the targeted non-Serb population of the Prijedor opstina. Your Honours, you will also have available to you the evidence from the experts such as Dr. Richard Wright, the professor of forensic anthropology who prepared the various reports of exhumations of bodies in Pasinac and Prijedor, and of a mass grave site in the village of Kevljani. Dr. John Clark is a forensic pathologist, who reported on the results of post-mortems carried out by him and his staff on bodies from Pasinac, Kevljani and Hrastava Glavica. You will have available the evidence and reports of Dr. Clark, Antony Brown, Judge Abdulmedzid Music, Dr. Eva Klonowski, as well as other forensic pathologists concerning their findings. These are not all the witnesses the Prosecution intends to call. In all, we anticipate that you will hear during the course of the Prosecution's case, from approximately 42 witnesses by way of viva voce evidence. The balance of the total of approximately 54 potential witnesses that we have selected as a representative sample of the available evidence will come in the form of transcript evidence from other proceedings or by way of expert reports, should the court permit it. It may be that Defence counsel will wish to cross-examine some of these witnesses, and they will appear before you in person. The evidence of others will likely be available to you in report form by consent of all counsel. Additionally, you will have for your consideration a number of binders of documents which have been filed and entered as exhibits, to my understanding, in these proceedings, to which reference will be made during the course of the trial. Your Honours, it is our respectful submission that at the end of the case, you will be satisfied that the Prosecution has tendered a body of evidence from which you will have no difficulty in determining that each accused is guilty of the charge -- as charged of the counts in the indictment relating to him. Unless Your Honours have any questions, that is the opening statement for the Prosecution.

During those times, Dragan Kolundzija became absolutely integrated in multiethnic society. Two other Muslims drivers at the same association said nothing to Kole but his friend was cursed and they were saying to him -- Mr. Kadijevic in those days was the supreme commander of the Yugoslav National Army and the conversation took place like this: "Have Kadeavic F expletive word you?
