Kole thought that this was just an insignificant banter, thinking that this colloquy between tolerant and extreme Muslims will never become a problem in Prijedor if secession is prevented elsewhere. After returning from Croatia, where the Kole had only been a driver and never came closer than two kilometres to the front lines, he resumed now his past haulage and was getting his informations only from Yutel, a television station that was based in Sarajevo and was produced and directed by a pro-Yugoslavia oriented Croatian man. Therefore, Kolundzija never thought that he would see a war in Prijedor. However, he was reassigned later to the reserve police unit to secure all civilians and that happened in late April of 1992. After Serb takeover of power in Prijedor, time passed uneventfully for Kolundzija, who provided sentry duty at public buildings. He never thought that Keraterm would be anything else than a ceramic tile factory. However, by following his orders, he found himself on the morning of June 3rd as a guard of detainees in the same factory. The detention centre, as it was then called by the Serbian police, was already set up and guarded by the military before his arrival there. Military also continued to provide additional outside perimeter guards at night. Kolundzija was during month of June an ordinary guard who raised questions of mistreatment of prisoners to his commander, Mr. Dzinko Knezevic, and constantly protested how much longer he is going -- this was going to go on, Keraterm and his assignment therein. The answers were three to four days and this will be over. He believed it since it seemed a very sincere answer by his commander. As that might seem insincere to you now, but I will ensure you, and we will present you evidence that recently discovered documents by this Defence counsel, pursuant to the request that was already before you, and this Trial Chamber has been informed about the discovery of the documents, will conclusively prove that Serbian authorities for Krajina disclosed existence of these prisons and prisoners within seven days of their establishment and three days after Kolundzija's assignment therein, to the international authorities, highest military and civilian officers on territory in Yugoslavia. They also requested medicine and foods and convoys to be established to Banja Luka and Krajina because Serbs were lacking them and were expecting that their stocks will not last more than a few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, it's approaching 1.00, time for the adjournment. Will you be bringing your closing to an end?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have -- I did think it was going to be 45 minutes but after the Prosecutor's statement, I believe I'll take about 15 minutes to comment on the acts that were allegedly committed by my client. So I might take a little longer. I would prefer if you would allow me to continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When we resume this afternoon, which will be at 2.30, after Mr. Vucicevic's presentation, I will deal with some administrative matters before we begin with the taking of the evidence. But there is one matter that concerns the Chamber, and I want to raise it now. The accused Sikirica is running a defence of alibi. He is saying he wasn't there. The Prosecution will be bringing witnesses who will say otherwise. As far as we can see, the accused Sikirica has not been identified before by these witnesses and the issue of his identification as the person who committed the crimes is obviously very crucial. It seems likely therefore that what will happen is that when the Prosecution witnesses come in, they will identify him, and the dangers of that kind of identification are well-known. I want counsel on both sides to prepare themselves to make submissions on that issue to the Chamber. Yes, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour was anticipating something I was literally about to get on my feet and say, that I had a short oral motion to make to you concerning this very topic, but it may be that it is sensible to deal with it. Not having raised the matter, we can make mutual submissions rather than me simply having to stand and make a motion orally to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was aware of it and I was going to deal with it before the first witness gave evidence this afternoon. I'm certainly alert to it. I warned my learned friend Mr. Ryneveld that I was going to make such a motion so he is not taken by surprise by the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will deal with it in the manner I have outlined. We will take the adjournment now and resume at 2.30 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I think you are in the last stages of your opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may proceed, please. As I said before the break, defence of Kolundzija has a document which depicts a meeting that took place in Belgrade on June 7th, 1992 where, from the Serbian authorities, Mr. Alexander Buha who was, at that time, a minister in the government was present and also in the government of government of Krajia, Mr. Lalovic was present where they have informed the highest authority of the United Nations in Yugoslavia at that time of existence of prisoners and their attempt to exchange those prisoners with the government of -- the Bosnian government, but they have received communication that they were not interested in exchange of those prisoners but that only they would accept food and arms and ammunition in exchange for Serbian prisoners. Then, the Serbian authorities requested that International Committee of Red Cross be informed. I think that directly counters the assertions that the Prosecutor has just stated in his opening. Also, Mr. Vulliamy who will testify for the Prosecution has indicated in one of the articles, one of the many articles that he has written that, indeed, international organisations and the governments had known from the very beginning of existence of these camps and merely that he has two months later reported about it. However, that was not hidden. The reason that I am bringing this up is there was no intent to harm these prisoners at the time that the camps were established. The situation became suddenly worse during the middle of July 1992. Kolundzija doesn't know why it happened. He only knows that a big group of prisoners was brought in one afternoon. He refused to admit them since the facility was overcrowded. He knew of the conditions that they were in, and he didn't want it aggravated. He was aware that they had pallets which the tiles were carried on that were only there instead of beds. However, at the beginning, Room 3 was used as the detention facility for the Serbians who were suspected of committing any crimes. Those prisoners also had nothing to lay on, and they were getting the same food and same pallets as the Muslim prisoners who were in the Rooms 1 and 2. Later on, as the number of the Muslims and Croatians who were in prison grew, that the detention room for the Serbians who were suspected of committing any crimes were -- was moved behind the Keraterm building. But still, conditions there were the same as they were in the rooms where the Muslims and Croatians were kept. Kolundzija didn't notice anything unusual on the evening of the 24th, just as the many witnesses, inmates that the Defence will produce will testify. Others the Prosecutor will produce, will testify as to the vague and unreliable acts of preparation, perhaps some that we will show have resulted from the years of mutual -- without any disparagement, recycling of the events, and perhaps with some motivation to aid in Prosecution of this case. As far as the night of the 24th of July, 1992 is concerned, although it's not disputed that massacre took place on the shift where Kolundzija had only de minimis authority to observe and report to the commanders, like on any other shift before, before any shooting occurred, he called the high-ranking police and military commanders to come in and restore order in the camp since the inmates began rioting. Commanders arrived at the scene and after that moment, Kolundzija had no command authority at all. It is expected that the evidence from the both Prosecution and Defence will show that he personally took no part in shooting. He was not in a position to control or stop the shooting from the arms which had been brought in by the soldiers, control having been taken from him by an army unit of much greater size and strength. He tried to stop the shooting and he tried to protect the detainees. As far as the indirect participation is concerned, it is agreed that the Prosecution -- with the Prosecution that criminal liability can only be established if a conduct is coupled with intent and that intent involves awareness of the act or participation coupled with a conscious decision to participate by planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the commission of crime. That was verbatim from the Tadic judgement. And that the Prosecution must prove that the accused contributed in some manner to the commission of the illegal act, or that he must distinguish himself by having done certain acts which are contrary to the alleged plan; and that is from the appeal judgement on Tadic. And we respectfully submit that Kolundzija has performed all those acts at all times without discrimination to those that he knew and those that he didn't. As a matter of fact, he helped many more of those that he didn't know because he was quite a secluded man before the war. He didn't know too many people, but whoever came and asked for his assistance, the assistance was never refused. Not even a single family member ever had been turned back when the food was brought in by the families. Kolundzija has been going around town picking up the food from the families of the detainees and bringing it to the centre. Kolundzija has taken detainees without knowing who they were, at the times there was no electricity in town, to the neighbouring well, and there would be 10 to 15 prisoners going, and sometimes it would be him or sometimes only one of the other guards taking all these people to get some cold water in the scorching heat of July. The guards, most of them reside in the neighbourhood. Discipline was not a discipline the way the military discipline was because they were a reserve police unit and they all went home to eat, most of them never reporting to the shift leaders, and therefore the food that was brought to the inmates at the same time - the food which was brought by the military by the way - was brought to the guards. Kolundzija on his own has asked the room leaders from all the rooms to find out who are the weak and underaged of the inmates and had given them that food to eat. No man who ever wanted to harm the prisoners would be giving the food, his food, because he didn't eat their food. He never went home to eat, so he took it away from his mouth to give it to the detainees. On two occasions, he had taken prisoners home to change, to see the families, all without asking any permission from anybody else, risking his position as a man who would be subjected to torture or who would be sent to the front line, to the most dangerous task and perhaps lose his life. Those thoughts were not present in his head. He did what he could to help, to help everybody, not just a few. He would allow inmates to use the phone to call home, and he would even discourage some of those whom he knew because he was not going to play favourites. And you will have witnesses who were inmates there whom Kole said, "No, you can't call today. Let somebody else call." There is no evidence that Kolundzija acted in any part of any common agreement with the local political leaders to commit offences as a part of either policy, if it allegedly existed. There was no evidence that Kole was -- as a shift leader, was a high or even an official rank giving superior authority with a power to punish guards so that he could give a signal of official tolerance to beating of -- or acts of persecution. While this seems a little strange here, but I think to explain any function we have to look into the practices of the society that existed at that time, and there is no meaning or word could be taken and directly translated. And the police at that time was considered to be from -- after years of worker self-management that was practised in Yugoslavia -- was supposed to be like a working unit, like a unit from a -- some government company, where 10 or 15 workers would have their leader, and that leader couldn't punish them, couldn't discipline them, he could only report to the higher ups who had all those authorities. Kole had a lot of respect for -- from his fellow guards because Kole, even when he was ordered to become shift leader, though unwillingly, accepted it because he knew that he could protect a lot more than by not accepting it and going away. There were those that he knew whom he became accustomed, shared their suffering, and he couldn't leave. He continued to help. There was never -- you will not hear in evidence ever that Kole called anybody out who was loaded on the trucks and later the remains of those were found. You will hear the evidence that Kole once was asked to find a few volunteers and he refused it and asked for a written order, and volunteers were not taken from his shift. Prosecutor is suggesting that on one night, Kole called somebody out, but our evidence is going to show that the only night when Kole went to a Room 2 was - and only once - to call out a prisoner who was brought and spent only one night and who is today alive and well and is alderman in the city of Prijedor. Prior to the conflict, he was the Captain in the Yugoslav army and became a military leader of the city of Kozarac. But Kole was nudged by his fellow guards. He went over there while all room, all detainees had "Cirkin, Cirkin, that's Kole. You can trust him. You can go out." And Kole went to talk because him and his guards never being in military action in Kozarac wanted to find out, curiosity what had happened. Mr. Cirkin, being a captain and a lawyer, a smart man that he is, careful, didn't come out. But in the morning, he did come out and the man who made him a cup of coffee was Dragan Kolundzija. The Defence denies that Kolundzija committed any crime. Any suggestion that he could have left his post had he been unwilling to continue at the camp shall be refuted that he was not a volunteer who could have withdrawn from his position while being an unranked guard or shift leader. He was a compulsory enlisted national serviceman assigned to the reserve police who had every reason to believe that had he deserted that post, he would be locked up and beaten to death in the camp just as it befell another Serb called Jovo Radocaj who was deemed to have been cooperating with the extremist Muslims or sent to the warfront to certain death, as I said earlier, or the most dangerous task possible. Furthermore, he could be of more help with reducing the suffering of detainees, many of whom, as I said, were his friends and he stayed. He stayed to help them. There is expected to be evidence from many, from Prosecution, that he was a good shift leader. Having stated the like of actus reus and mens rea still most importantly the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that Kolundzija was directly or indirectly a knowing and willing participant in the offences set out in the indictment. We respectfully submit that the Prosecutor will fall short in meeting his burden of proof on all elements of the crimes that he is charged. Since the evidence will turn out as stated, then Dragan Kolundzija would be entitled to the acquittal at the end of the Prosecutor case in chief. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. I turn now to deal with a number of matters prior to the taking of evidence. The first is that there is a schedule which should have been distributed. Have you received it, with the dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If this is the schedule that was produced some weeks ago, yes, we do have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, there is a more up-to-date --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We have a scheduling order with a list of when the courts will be sitting, et cetera, et cetera, but that was at least ten days ago. I haven't received anything further, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it has been revised. I'll see that it is distributed. But for the immediate time, it is necessary for me to say that the Chamber will not be sitting on Friday, the 23rd of March, there being a diplomatic reception, nor will the Chamber sit on the 30th of March, Friday the 30th of March. So the first two Fridays the Chamber will not sit. I will see to it that this is distributed, the most up-to-date schedule immediately after we adjourn today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Secondly, there is a motion from Mr. Vucicevic to be allowed to use the language of the witness, B/C/S. I am to say that there is no need for such a motion, since the Rules permit this. Next, the question of transcripts. There is a motion from the Prosecution to admit transcripts in respect of six witnesses. The practice that has developed in the Tribunal, and which we intend to adopt, is to have the Prosecution distribute the whole transcript, marking the relevant areas so that we know what are the areas which are identified as relevant. We would need three copies in English and two in French, and the Prosecution will have two weeks to accomplish that. I observe that there is no response from Sikirica on this particular matter. You may want to give some thought to that if indeed you intend to make a response. In respect of the witness Vulliamy, the motion to have access to his notes, tapes, and so on, that will be dealt with at the same time that we deal with the transcripts, the admissibility of the transcripts. Now, the Prosecution is to complete its case by June 1st. That's in a period of ten weeks, and we will sit longer hours if that is necessary. This, of course, requires the cooperation of all parties, the Prosecution and the Defence, to ensure that the necessary discipline and rigor is applied to the case, confining questions to relevant areas. I see the Prosecution has submitted 14 witnesses for the first two weeks, and I think that's a very good aim. We only need to see that it is accomplished. The 58 includes the six transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It does. You will keep under review, as we go along, as will the Chamber, the whole question of relying on Rule 92 bis and, where necessary, avoiding viva voce evidence. Those are the matters I wanted to raise before we turn to the question that I raised before in respect of which we'll have submissions from both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, yes, since you indicated you were going to do an oral motion, we'll start with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful. You were -- can I first of all start by addressing you on what is the law of this Tribunal in relation to this particular topic. Your Honour, a perusal of the Rules will reveal that there is -- the Rules of Procedure and Evidence will reveal that there is no specific rule which deals specifically and authoritatively with this issue. That being so, I respectfully submit that Your Honours have to fall back on four provisions in order to see what is the basis for admitting or excluding the kind of evidence that I anticipate the Prosecutor will seek to adduce. Those four provisions are Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute and Rules 89 and 95 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I'm sure Your Honours will forgive me if I briefly remind you of the text of those Rules and the relevant parts thereof. Article 20, subparagraph 1, "The Trial Chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair," and that's an article which is headed, "Commencement and Conduct of Trial Proceedings." Article 21 headed rights of the accused subparagraph 2, "In the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing." Rule 89 is in section 3 of the Rules, Rules of Evidence, and it's headed, "General Provisions". And the first four paragraphs A to D are, we submit, relevant to this issue. Paragraph A, "A Chamber shall apply the rules of evidence set forth in this section and shall not be bound by national rules of evidence." Subparagraph B, "In cases not otherwise provided for in this section, a Chamber shall apply Rules of Evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law." Subparagraph C, "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." D, "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." And finally, Rule 95, is headed "Exclusion of Certain Evidence." It reads, "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to, and would seriously damage, the integrity of the proceedings." There has -- and I'm recalling this off the top of my head, there has been one particular instance where the issue has been referred to in a judgement of the Tribunal. That was in the first case before the Tribunal involving the Prosecutor versus Tadic. My recollection is that in the judgement, there was a brief reference to in-court identifications which were admitted but to which, and I think the phrase used was, "very little weight as attached." Your Honour, we submit that the process of conducting an in-court identification is one which is inherently unfair, both generally and in the particular context of this Tribunal. What is the nature of the process? In most legal systems, if one is to judge by that which one sees on television, seem to have a separate area where accused persons are detained for the purposes of a trial. The accused sits either in a dock, for example, as it's known in the English system, or at a separate table. Almost always, he is flanked, he or she is flanked by uniformed court officers or police officers or guards. For an astute and alert witness, it is never going to be terribly difficult for that person to pick out where in the courtroom an accused person is sitting. I'll come to the specific example of this court layout in a moment. There are some particular issues which affect this Tribunal in our submission. The first is this: As part of the process of investigating, detaining and trying suspects and accused, there is a widespread dissemination, both in the world and in particular in the former Yugoslavia, of images of either arrested or wanted persons. There are wanted posters disseminated all over the country. And if I may be forgiven for a moment for giving evidence before you, I've certainly been in Bijelina and Brcko and have seen such posters in some places. There is broadcast of court proceedings - and again I've been staying in hotels where Bosnian television has had quite substantial sections of proceedings before the Tribunal being broadcast, and I think there is in fact a weekly programme which is a digest of what has happened recently before the Tribunal. And I have no doubt that, for example, given the importance of today's -- this case, there will be some coverage in the former Yugoslavia of today's proceedings before you. There are sites on the Internet which have on them images of accused and wanted people. They are readily accessible by anybody with a modicum of expertise in searching the Internet. I turn now to the physical layout of this courtroom. The witness of course sits here. Looking around this room, Your Honours will notice that there are remarkably few people who aren't in fact either uniformed or robed, either in the robes of the international Tribunal or the robes of the bar of the Netherlands or robes of their national jurisdictions. And of course, my learned friend, Mr. Ryneveld and his colleagues sit there. They are obviously not going to be accused people. There is a line of very obviously lawyerish looking people here, also wearing robes, with the exception of our interpreter but she, of course, is a woman. There are members of the registry all wearing robes of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and then there are Your Honours who are obviously dressed somewhat differently from the rest of us. There are four people at present sitting behind the Prosecutor. One is a lady obviously doing court reporting, and three gentlemen at the far side. There is a guard just to my immediate left, and then behind us there we have the accused, each flanked by a guard in blue uniform. We submit that a witness who comes and sits in this court is not going to find it very difficult to see where it is the accused, whether they be one in number or three in number, are sitting, and it's not going to be terribly difficult for him to have a try at picking out who he's been invited to pick out. So given all those people, we say that the process is one which is inherently unfair. In one case in which I was involved, that process was made even more unfair when the learned Presiding Judge in the Tribunal started to come in in the mornings and actually tell the witnesses where the accused were sitting in the court and would point him out, and so the unfairness of it became compounded. The next thing we submit is this: That in this proceeding -- in the procedure of identifying an accused or a suspect, there are available to the Prosecution - indeed to the Defence if they want to do it - much more satisfactory and much fairer means of conducting identifications. Three come to mind but it's not an exhaustive list: the identification parade, the photo spread or photo board, or identification by a series of video images being presented to an accused. Each of those, provided they are conducted in a reasonably disciplined and well-structured way, is inherently fairer than the procedure which my learned friend will propose to Your Honours as being appropriate. They are available and easy to carry out and there is no reason, we submit, why they shouldn't be carried out with any witness if the Prosecution so chooses. At the very least, the Prosecution ought to exhaust those means first in order to establish what the position is as regards any particular witness. What I'd like very, very briefly to do, Your Honour -- and I do this not in order to suggest to Your Honours that the English system is the best and one that you should adopt automatically, I'm not doing it for that purpose at all. I'm doing it simply to give you an idea of how the law in England developed and why, because my submission is that it's now developed to an extent where a reasonably sensible and well-accepted procedure exists. In the 1970s there were a number of troubling cases which came before the Court of Appeal involving identification evidence, and there was one particular notorious case involving a man who is now a government minister who was on trial for robbery and where the issue of identification evidence became important. And it was in that way that the matter came before the public for more general discussion. The upshot of it was that a considerable amount of Court of Appeal activity then took place in order to give guidance both to the courts and to practitioners and to the police as to the fairest and best means of conducting identification procedures and admitting identification evidence before the court. One of the consequences of that procedure -- of that development was that the Attorney General announced that prosecutors instructed by him would no longer seek to identify in court for the first time an accused or a suspect. The past 25 years have seen considerable development in relation to the law of identification for criminal cases. The present position is that there now exists an extensive code of practice, code of conduct for identification procedures. It's set out in all the up-to-date textbooks for practitioners, the most obvious of which comes to mind is one called Archibald, which I know is in the library here to consult it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry. That code of conduct provides, as I say, strict rules of procedure. The consequences of failing to follow properly the procedure, if the failure to follow is a substantial one, is that the evidence is almost always excluded, but it depends on each individual case. Observance of the rules is not rigid. There is certainly one decided case where the police were having difficulties assembling enough people from the public to conduct an identification parade so what they did was put a video in a corridor of a police station which had a large number of people passing and repassing along it and at one stage allowed the defendant to come along that corridor. The video was then shown to the witnesses and the Court of Appeal decided that that was not an unfair procedure and was therefore admissible. I understand that in the former Yugoslavia there certainly is some form of identification parade procedure. It may well be that either my learned friend Mr. Londrovic or Mr. Petrovic could assist Your Honours if you wanted information about that system. Your Honours, in conclusion what we submit is this: Of course such evidence may satisfy the test of relevance. The issue of identity is plainly relevant in this case. But we say this: The evidence is not probative of really terribly much given the particular physical constraints that I've pointed out and the circumstances to which I have adverted. At best it demonstrates the ability of someone to pick out a fish in a barrel. Even if it is probative, we would respectfully submit, that it would be appropriate to apply Rule 89(d) and Rule 95 and say that this evidence is really not particularly reliable and it is sufficiently unreliable that it ought not to be admitted. And secondly, that given the very nature of the exercise that is conducted and to which I have pointed out, it is inherently unfair and therefore falls foul of those provisions to which I have alluded, Articles 20 and 21 and Article 89(a). Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, your submission then is that there should be no dock identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour has it in one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a distinction, is there not, between the case in which a witness identifies somebody after what's often called a fleeting glance?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Classically the case of a mugging in a street in which the whole thing happens within a few seconds and the accused is gone -- or the perpetrator is gone. It is particularly those cases which are the causes of concern, as I think you'll agree. Now, there is a distinction between that sort of case and the case where the witness knows the accused, has known him over a long time, and a case, which may be the case here, I don't know, in which the accused says, "Well, I was in this camp for three months, I got to know X or Y." And then it's simply a question of recognition rather than identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the circumstances may vary. Any of these circumstances may apply to this case, but isn't it a case really where the Trial Chamber are going to have to look at what it is which is sought to be proved rather than making a blanket order? That is, having to look at each case to see what the Prosecution are asking us to do, rather than to make a blanket order at the very beginning which may be unfair on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think there are two points, if I may say so. The first is this: The problem of widespread dissemination of images of the accused - and indeed I see today that yet further photographs are being taken of him on two occasions today in the court. That is the real danger is that someone may see an image on a television or some other place and is simply recognising a picture that he's seen of the accused who is identified to him on the television as Sikirica. That's the danger. And he may do it unconsciously. He may simply see the picture, listen to the news broadcast out of interest, not realising the importance of what he is doing and unconsciously pick the man out as a result of that. That's the difference. The second point is this: Of course, there are cases of recognition or cases of fleeting glances, and those are important. One of the factors that we have to consider here, and it is relevant in our submission, is this is not a case which is appearing before the courts six months after the events which are being described. We are talking about a case which is coming before you after nearly nine years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those are matters that would affect the weight to be given to the evidence. We would have to assess matters like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, but it also goes part and parcel of what I call particular issues affecting this Tribunal, and I perhaps should have adverted to that as well earlier on. If one takes all those factors together, then the process begins to look, in our submission, inherently unfair and potentially unfair on each occasion, we submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do any other of Your Honours have any questions that I could answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no more questions. Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At the outset it appears that the issues raised by Judge May with my learned friend actually outline exactly the proposal that I had in terms of a response to my learned friend's submission. I have here that there is the issue of recognition witnesses versus identification witnesses. And that each case, we would respectfully submit, turns on its own unique and individual facts for each witness. There are a number of witnesses, as will become obvious from the summaries that will be provided, who knew the accused or some of them, before the conflict, knew them intimately, and of course, for those witnesses, the issue of recognition would be straightforward but for the passage of some nine years. My friend's issue about the unfairness of perhaps witnesses having seen images on the media can of course be dealt with properly by appropriate examination in chief and cross-examination about what the witness had seen, all of which the court can take into consideration in making the determination as to whether or not the witness is in fact recalling who they saw back in 1992 or whether it's -- their memory has been refreshed by other images later. Another issue my friend has raised of course is the structure of this courtroom and that there are only -- that the only persons not somehow robed or somehow in uniform are the accused at the back of the courtroom. This is different again of course, and this is a very minor point but it isn't a single accused. There are three different accused and it may well be that witnesses may confuse one with the other so there is the additional factor of three different people, not just one person. That is a very minor issue but it's a point. His lordship Judge May raised the issue of not a fleeting glimpse. That's exactly my point in this case, that most of these witnesses you will hear were in the camp over a two month or more period and met these people on rotating shifts. Every 12 hours these people appeared, time and time and time again. Some of them knew them before the conflict. Some of them knew them during the conflict. Some of them were identified by the accused as, "I'm so and so." Others heard, you will find, hearsay evidence from others who did know them who said, "That's so and so." That is hearsay for the person. However, over a period of time, if you have someone introduced to you, the inherent difficulty is that the introduction is wrong. But nevertheless, if you are with that person, you can identify who that person is, at least in terms of the name that you had that person introduced to you as. So what I'm saying there is it's not a fleeting glimpse. Over a period of time they will recognise the individual and be able to pick out, perhaps, which individual that they were dealing with. They may be wrong about the name to be ascertained, but at least the image would stand out in their recollection over that period of time. As I say, our view is, with the greatest of respect, that it's a matter of weight for each individual, and not a matter of admissibility, per se. The witnesses I anticipate will describe the individuals that they recall to the best of their recollection. Many of the descriptions they gave were given in statements, which the Defence counsel have, many years ago, closer to the time and the event. They often were asked, when they gave their original statements, to give a general description of what the person looked like. Finally, this procedure that I'm familiar with has been used before other Trial Chambers at this Tribunal in the Foca cases, both the Kunarac, et al. and Krnojelac that is presently going on. Evidence of in-court identification has been admitted. The issue of weight, of course, has depended on each individual instance. In the Kunarac decision, I do recall that there was some counts that were dismissed because the court indicated that they placed very little probative weight on certain in-court identifications, but there were other witnesses who were able to testify as to how long they had seen the person over a period of time. It's all a matter of weight. Accordingly, our submission is that we be allowed to deal with each of the witnesses, elicit the basis for their knowledge for identification and be allowed to indicate if they are recognition witnesses or otherwise. Again, it's a matter of weight for this Court to place on. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So all your witnesses would fall into the category of persons who knew the accused before, it's a question of recognition or, in any event, they would have spent a period of about two months in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: With the opportunity to have observed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. With those people who didn't know them before the war, there is the additional difficulty that they may have been told the name of the individual and the person who told them could have been wrong about the name. But nevertheless, they will be able to identify what person they are talking about because they've seen them and seen them committing certain acts that they will testify to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But your point really is that each witness should be dealt with individually and we should approach it on a separate basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is our submission on behalf of the Prosecution, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any reply, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There's only one issue. My learned friend hasn't dealt with this issue which is one of the other more satisfactory, what I submit are more satisfactory methods of conducting identification. I think the simplest here is the photo board. Why those are not appropriate, why the short circuit method of identifying someone in the, what we submit, is the unsatisfactory conditions of court is the first option, the option of choice, rather than the more satisfactory one of the photo board which is one which we are familiar with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In order to maximize our time, the Chamber will not rule on the matter now. We'll proceed to hear the first witness, but we'll stop short when we come to the question of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, before we call the first witness who would propose to be K3, there is one other issue that has to be dealt with before the witness is called into the courtroom. As you know, there are applications or there have been successful applications for protected measures and many of the witnesses have been given pseudonyms. It has come to my attention that it was anticipated that with the pseudonym comes the obvious protected measure that there would be facial distortion for these witnesses, otherwise a pseudonym makes no sense. However, looking at some of the documentation that may have been taken for some of the earlier witnesses, it wasn't specified that the Prosecution was seeking the protected measure of the distortion of the face. I'm not asking for voice distortions. We're asking that with the pseudonym come obviously a distortion of the image for the television screen, otherwise it would make no sense to simply have a pseudonym issued. We would ask this Court to orally, at this point, permit us to have facial distortion for the television screen to further protect the witness' identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that for all the witnesses in respect for whom you are seeking protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The witnesses whom have been granted the pseudonyms. There are, I believe, only three that have been granted closed session proceedings. I'm talking about the others. There are a number of witnesses for whom there are no protected measures but, unfortunately, in some of the -- there were a matter of about three or four different phases of requests for protected measures and some of the latter ones I believe that we did ask for facial distortion, but in some of the earlier ones, that was not requested. I take it my learned friends would have no objection to facial distortion since it makes no sense to give a pseudonym without protecting the witness in that case. I understand that a facial distortion takes no time with the AV people. Voice distortion does actually run into some time. They have to take a voice image for each particular witness, and that takes about 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm not clear about is when the protection was granted and the pseudonym was granted, are you saying that it wasn't specified whether it would be in respect of facial distortion or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It wasn't specified in the request. The Court granted the request that was put, but the request didn't specify that with the pseudonym, we were also asking for facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you are now making that request?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I am now making that request, because that's the only request that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you would have to make it in respect of each witness as the witness comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to comment on what my learned friend says. As I look at the list of witnesses which we received, we shall be having 23 witnesses. Only 7 of them have not asked for pseudonym. I do not object in principle but, as you have just said, why do we not do it from case to case, that is to hear individual explanations for the application for protective measures because evidently the majority of testimony shall be heard under some protective measures, that will turn this into its own contradiction, that is, it seems that hearing will cease to be public. Excessive resorts to protective measures, I'm afraid, compromises the principle of public hearing. So therefore, we do not object in principle to a more restrictive approach. We should like to hear, in each individual case, why protective measures are sought. Therefore, we do not object in principle, but we do object to the application of such matters on a large scale, that only 7 of the 23 have not sought to testify under protection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic is right in one respect. The Chamber never intended to make a global grant. It will be -- each case will be considered on its own merits, and the Prosecution will have to make a case for it. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, just for clarification purposes, the witnesses that I understand are affected by this, because this -- we do have actual protective measures for some of the later applications. There is only four affected that we did not, that's K3, the first witness, K4, K6, and K13. So there are four for whom we do not have specific rulings because they were done some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your first witness is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: K3. So the very first witness we require -- we are making an application for facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. On what grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In order to adequately respond to that, I wonder whether we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you show that to the witness, please? Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are in private [sic] session. Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you show the piece of paper in your hand to the witness, please? First of all, witness, do you see your name on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your birthday immediately behind your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that you know, you will now be referred to in these proceedings as Witness A. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that document be marked as an exhibit in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness A, I understand that you were born and raised in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand, witness, that you attended school there and you graduated from school in about 1971. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you just sit a little closer to the microphones so the translators can hear your voice, witness? Just move the chair up. Speak into those microphones, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, I understand as well that during 1972 and 1973, you spent about 15 months in the army as a driver, and then after you left the army, you became employed in Prijedor as a merchant. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked for the same company, sir, until an event that occurred on the 29th of May of 1992, when your wife came to the store where you were working and told you something. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that day, sir, that changed events for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That day, my wife worked for Patrija, and my shop was not far from Patrija. We did not have a telephone. So that my wife came around 4.00 in the afternoon and she said, "Come quickly, turn over the business, count the money, lock the shop. We have just heard that Hambarine would be shelled."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, may I just bring to the attention of the Defence counsel that one of the virtues of the witness summary is that it allows the other counsel to look at it and to indicate whether it objects to leading in respect of any particular paragraphs, and we proceed more expeditiously that way. So you can proceed but I just want to bring that to the attention of counsel on the other side, that you indicate in the future if you have objections to what paragraphs you wish counsel not to lead on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it the invitation is that I lead until my learned friends perhaps -- well, I appreciate myself that there will be certain areas where I simply won't lead but unless my friends object, I will assume that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't think that was Your Honour's invitation at all. I have not discussed this particular summary with my learned friend and I don't want him to assume on this occasion that he can lead willy-nilly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I understand that -- as a result of what your wife said, did you go back to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen two days later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Two days later, while I was at home, I was arrested together with my brother. They shoved us on to a bus and took us to Omarska. When we arrived in Omarska, when we fetched up in front of the gate, the policeman said that there was no more room in Omarska, said, "Give us four men to slaughter them and take this vehicle wherever you like." But nobody got off the bus. We then turned back and went to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That sort of is a very broad summary of what occurred. I'm going to ask you to back up a little bit and fill in some details, if you would. And perhaps I can address your mind to the areas that I'm interested in. Now, while you were on the 31st of May, is that the date that you indicate that soldiers came to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. It was around 4.00 in the afternoon. Around 1.00, I had been called by a friend of mine, Dragan Babic and told me to put up a white flag on my house, and all the members of the family should put on white arm bands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, as if to show our loyalty to our town, to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Were you -- did you know what was about to happen when you received that phone call, in terms of the things that eventually did happen? Were you told what to expect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: All he said was that some troops would come by, and of course I couldn't even imagine, I couldn't even make a guess as to what might happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, did troops actually come to your house in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you and your brother were arrested? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We were having lunch, and I jokingly told my brother, "Well, help yourself, well, it just could be of use," even though of course I had no idea as to what might happen. All of a sudden I heard a bang on the door and a voice shouting, "All males outside with your hands up." And this is what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you find out where that voice was coming from? Were there people, soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They were soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms and, as I came through the passage, I raised my hands. My mother was standing in the courtyard and crying and saying, "Where are you taking these children?" And a soldier came up to my mother, hugged her and said, "Don't worry, they will just be questioned and will be back home in no time at all."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The soldiers, were they armed? Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They all had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you recognise any of the individuals who were involved in your arrest, the arrest of you and your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I knew some of those men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know the ethnicity of the men who were involved in your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the names of the individuals who you then recognised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There was Dragan Skoric. Cigo, the taxi driver from Omarska. There was Tica. There was Uzelac, Branko Uzelac. There was -- there were many. They were many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you refer to a taxi driver. Did you see any of these taxi drivers -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer, Witness A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I saw a number of men. I saw Dragan Skoric. I saw Uzelac. I saw Celica. I saw Cigo from Omarska, a taxi driver there. I saw Tica from Omarska. I saw a man in a black uniform whose name was Joja. They were many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the individuals who were involved in the arrest later on? You've told us that you eventually went to Keraterm. Did you see any of those individuals in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Of them, the only one I saw was the man in black uniform, who had bandoliers over his chest and everybody called him Joja. He arrived in Keraterm two days later. He went into the dormitory, put down his weapons, and asked, "Is there anyone from a village near Bosanski Novi?" And the name of the village was -- just a moment. The name of the village escapes me. Maybe it will come back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: But two men answered, two men responded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. While you were being arrested, could you hear any military sounds in the distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. I heard something like tank grenades. It is above my house, about 150 to 200 metres above my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you find out what caused -- or what resulted from those sounds of the tank grenades that you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The result of these shells were that they hit a house with about eight to nine people in it. They were all killed. And the hodza was allowed to bury them. From what I heard after I came out of the camp, that hodza took photographs of it all and he supposedly has pictures of the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, sir, when you talk about a hodza is that a Muslim priest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. All right. Now, sir, you've told us about you and your brother being arrested at your home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you in fact dealt with once you were arrested by the soldiers? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They told us to put our hands behind our heads, to put our heads down, and to walk towards buses that were parked there. When we reached the buses, the driver was already in his seat and there was a soldier. He took our rings, our change that we had, money, cigarettes, everything that we had in our pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that, sir, after all your possessions were taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: After that, he would not allow us to take seats in the bus so we had to sit on the floor. And the man in the black uniform, whose name was Joja then boarded the bus and asked us why we were sitting on the floor of the bus, why weren't we sitting in the seats? And we answered that it was that soldier who had ordered us to sit like that. Then (redacted) [phoen] whom I know very well, [redacted], who also came on board the bus and took out 200 marks. When the man in the black uniform saw him robbing us, he hit him forcefully, he gave this money back to Muhamed and the rest of the money he took as evidence and put in the boot of a parked Mercedes and he took a driver and that guy, the soldier, put them in the Mercedes and told them to drive to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, while you were put on the bus, were you personally beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I personally was not, but I saw it with my own eyes how they ill-treated and beat my neighbour, Hasan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so just so that I've got it clear, you and your brother and about how many other men are on these buses at this point, at -- in Prijedor near your home at Donja Puharska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were about 50 or maybe 60 of us in that bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As far as I could see, there were six of them. Not all the buses were parked in the same place. My bus, that is there were two of them, and they were at the cross roads in Donja Puharska, and the buses were parked by the mosque and there was a third group of buses in Orlakica Soka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the buses that you and your brother got on, those were parked close to your house, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the buses took off, I understand, sir, and I understand that you were brought to Omarska, and as you did that, you passed through the village of Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way through Kozarac on the 31st of May on the way to Omarska, what, if anything, did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I saw many killed people, killed livestock, cows, horses, and I even saw something that I shall never forget, that I shall never forget, a man who was placed -- killed a man who was placed as a scarecrow next to the -- by the road. There were many killed people. The houses were still burning. They were still smoking. There were houses which were intact but those were the houses that belonged to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You eventually arrived at Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you told us early in your summary that you arrived at Omarska and you were told that there was no room at that camp for you and that that policeman said something to the driver; what was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. He said to the driver, "Give me four to slaughter them and the rest of them take them where you like."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what happened to your bus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I'm sorry to interrupt you. We will, with the indulgence of the interpreters, continue up to 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left Omarska and you took -- you went somewhere and I'm going to lead here. I understand you eventually ended up at Keraterm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when your bus arrived at Keraterm, sir, where did you -- where do you arrive? Was there a location at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. We entered the Keraterm compound and when we arrived, the order came to get off, stand by the wall, face the wall, and put your hands against the wall and spread your legs, spread your feet. I did that, and a soldier then came up and hit me on the head, cursed me, and said, "How do you hold your hands?" And I said, "Well, against the wall, as you said." He said, "No, only with three fingers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I may have missed it, but did you say he did something to you when you did it with five fingers?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this moment, I would like to object, this is asked and answered. The first time I passed it because when there were invitation for a slaughter of some civilians, but this is second time that he is asking witness to repeat previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understood him to be seeking a clarification as to testimony that had been given by the witness. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand my question, sir. You told us you got instructions about using three fingers instead of five fingers. In addition to getting instructions, did anything else happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. When I had put my hands against the wall, not knowing that I should do it with three fingers, I had my whole palms of my hand against the wall, and he hit me on the back of my head and said, "How are your hands three fingers? That was the order, three fingers only."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you arrived at Keraterm, are you able to recall whether you then knew any of the people that were at Keraterm when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, who, if anyone, that you may have recognised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I knew Tomica, Dragan, Kole, Civerica, brothers Banovic and a number of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those people were there upon your arrival; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time of the day was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: It was around half past 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were told to lean against the wall, did anything else happen with respect to you and the other prisoners in terms of any documents you may have had on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: As we were leaning with our hands against the wall, they searched us and everything, our ID cards, and driver's licences, and passports, all these were taken and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after you were searched and had your documents taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Then we were told to enter a room with a very narrow door and, as we were going in, there was a soldier next to the door and struck each one of us with his rifle on the back. But I was lucky, I passed through very quickly so that I missed the blow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the room number you were placed in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Room 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in Room 2 during your entire stay in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after some time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I moved to Room 1. All those who were taken for interrogation from Room 2, after the interrogation, they would be taken to Room 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother, [redacted], was he also with you in Room 2 at first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He was, yes. We were all. All of us who arrived in Keraterm, we were all in Room 2. We were the first to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this Room 2, do you remember approximately how large that room was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, it was larger than any other room in Keraterm. Later on there were between 550 to 580 people in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to describe for this Court the approximate size of that room in terms of say this courtroom, would it be bigger than this courtroom? If so, how many times bigger? If smaller, how much smaller? Can you look around this courtroom and give the Court some idea of the size of Room 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, of course. From that corner to the middle, and it could have been some 15 metres long. And on the side where I was the first time, there were iron bars and one could see parts of some vehicles or some machines, that is, they were wrecks or something or shelves and those parts were on those shelves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The length of the room, if you were sitting where you were now and you are looking towards where Their Honours are, you've told us that it was about 15 metres wide. The distance between you and the Judges, are you able to give us an estimate of how long that is or ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Not 15 metres wide. Long, I think, 15 metres long. It was like entering a tunnel. You could not see the far corner, but it was narrow. It could have been 6 to 8 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 6 to 8 metres wide and in terms of the total size of this courtroom, would you say that the total area was bigger or smaller or about the same as this courtroom. Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was slightly, slightly larger. Slightly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you were moved to Room 1, that would be -- was that as large as Room 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No, it was smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give the Court an assessment in terms of the size of, again, this courtroom, how large Room 1 was in comparison to this courtroom you are now sitting in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: What I can say is that it was about 12 times 4 metres, 4 wide. So three pallets could fit in and they were 1.1, metre and a half, and three of these wooden pallets could fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question slightly. I understand you've told us in terms of pallets and metres. In terms of the size of this courtroom, would Room 1 be larger than, smaller than or about the same as this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, about this courtroom, perhaps slightly narrower, perhaps slightly narrower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we'll have to get some information on the size of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely. I just thought I -- I'm not done with the witness and other witnesses will, in fact, be providing some sketches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Room 2 before you went to Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In Room 2, I was there some 11 or 12 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were at Keraterm, do you know how many shifts there were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: There were three shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if and when they changed and, if so, at what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do know. In the morning, from 6.00 in the morning until 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the order of the shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really know the order, but I should say it was Fustar's shift first, then Kole's shift, and then Kajin's shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who any of the guards were on those respective shifts, for example, do you know who was on Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I know Batan. He was Kole's deputy. I know him. And then Dugi, I couldn't give you any other names because whoever had a uniform could enter the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about Room 1 something further. When you were in Room 1 after 11 or 12 days in Room 2, can you tell us how many men would be housed in Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: In that room there were about 30 to 40 men when I came there, but a much larger number of men had been interrogated, because some people allegedly went home. And all of a sudden, an order came that nobody was to move anywhere and then some of those same people were caught again and brought back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, will you find a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Do you want to stop now or just finish, perhaps, paragraph 9 and stop at that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you started paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have -- I was about to, yes, I sort of have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think we have done 15 minutes with the indulgence of the interpreters, and we shouldn't trespass further.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll continue with paragraph 9 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take the adjournment now until --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just with Your Honours' indulgence, I raised at a Status Conference the issue of communication by counsel with the witness after the oath has been taken and evidence has begun. I don't think we have arrived at a definitive position. May we know what Your Honours would wish us to do? I would urge that there be no communication save with the leave of the Court after the oath has been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the procedure. Witness A, you are not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that includes the counsel for the Prosecution. Thank you. We adjourn, 9.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
